David Friedberg: France’s Crisis Is a Warning for America

“France is a bellwether for the West.

So take a look at this chart. This chart is a measure of public spending as a percent of GDP.

And you can see the comparison of France's public spending as a % of GDP to the peak public spending as a % of GDP of major communist nations.”

@Chamath:

“So do you think France is a communist state? They spend like it.”

@Jason:

“Well, it's certainly been a socialist state, right?”

Chamath:

“Is it working?”

@Friedberg:

“That's my point. And I think this is such a prescient lesson for the West to look at.

We all think that there's some political problem with Macron or whoever it was.

The more the government spends, the worse the conditions get for its people, not the opposite, and then the people riot and revolt.

Take a guess where the US is today. US public spending is roughly 36% of GDP. France today is operating its national government spending deficit is 5.4% of GDP. The US is actually 6.2% of GDP.

France is, I think, probably the first to go because they're only growing their economy at half a percent while the US is growing at 2.3%.

So we're still kind of hanging on because we have some degree of economic growth that's allowing us to kind of hold things together.

But I would argue that we are facing the same sort of fiscal cliff which leads to this extraordinary social unrest as France.

All the economic measures are aligned, we're at the same rate, we're at the same set of problems, and we're starting to see the cracks in the system.

There's probably a multi-year solution.”

1/ On Squiggle #6529
 
I would like to explain why we are excited about “buying a Squiggle” 
 
While Squiggles are, in fact, sweet, the exciting part is that every part of this process happened in a decentralized manner.
 
2/ @aRegularDad proposed a Meme Card to fund a Squiggle acquisition.

81 profiles participated in the Main Stage vote and voted with TDH to mint this as a Meme Card

The card won. 77 paid editions were minted, providing 2.51 ETH for the acquisition.
 
3/  @cheesebiz  and @bankons helped scout and connected @squiggleDAO . SquiggleDAO suggested trying to acquire Squiggle 6529
 
The price was 3.01 ETH, so @MadaCollects who had been following the discussion, chipped in another 0.5 ETH to the pool (respect!)
 
4/ The seller wanted to stay anonymous, preserve the provenance (no intermediary transfers) and keep their vault secure.

Ultimately, the seller trusted SquiggleDAO and 6529 network and sent the Squiggle directly to the 6529 Network Museum before receiving payment.

5/ Reminder: What is the 6529 network museum? It is a SAFE vault organized by TDH, owned by the network, a cultural asset, NFTs go in, but ~they do not go out. 
 
It is the network-native concept of a national public museum
 
6/ Finally, one more step to replace the temporary art on the card with something appropriate for the long-term. Well, another TDH vote of course.
 
@ricardotakamura  won with THE VAULT, a long-exposure light painting made at Casa NUA in Brazil.
 
7/ So to recap:
- Decentralized network mints a meme card to buy a squiggle
- Decentralized network picks which squiggle to buy
- Decentralized network updates the art
- Decentralized network permanent home for the squiggle
 
8/ What was my contribution to any step of this project? 

Nothing at all. I was not involved at all in any way. 

I had a vague awareness that it was happening, but was not following any of the details, let alone helping.
 
9/ Now, some of you are thinking “ok, fine, that is cute, the NFT nerds are collecting NFTs again”
 
Maybe.

David Friedberg: We’ve Lost the Plot on Immigration

“If you're providing social services to an immigrant population, then that's not necessarily a productive immigrant population in terms of being able to contribute to growing the economy and supporting civil society.

But if a population of immigrants come in and they're productive, meaning they can get jobs and they can work, and they can support themselves, that means they're adding something positive to the economy, to the civil society, and that is the sort of selection criteria that needs to take place.

So that's a simple framework for determining whether or not you should do this, and an easy way to solve it is get rid of social services for immigrants.

As soon as you get rid of social services for immigrants, then you self-select into the right population that's going to come in.

It's not about assimilating to society. It's about sharing the values of what makes the United States, the United States.

The values of, what do we actually care about, what are the principles that we all share as a civil society of the United States or a civil society of France, is a screening criteria that seems to have been thrown out the window.”

Jason:

“Do you believe in Freedom of speech? Do you believe in the Second Amendment?”

Friedberg:

“Do you believe that women are equal to men?

Do you believe that you should work for your money as opposed to take it from the government?

Do you believe in your individual rights?

Is your church paramount to the government and the laws of the state?

And do you believe that other people have rights that you don't get to trample on?

Those are the sorts of things that are, in many cases, counter to the cultural, religious, and other traditional beliefs of certain populations that end up causing the damage in the West, and I think that it's been kind of completely lost in the process.”

Drawdowns are the norm. New highs are the exception.

Historically the S&P 500 has spent ~80–95% of its time below a prior peak. Since 1871, 82% of months were underwater (price basis). Since 1950, only about 7% of trading days were at record highs.

Volatility is the price of admission. You cannot earn equity-like long-term returns with bond-like volatility; there is no free lunch. The temporary discomfort of being below your high-water mark is the cost of capturing the upside over decades.

That’s why staying the course matters for investors:

• Markets trend higher over time, but the path is jagged. Recoveries eventually erase most drawdowns. 
• Selling during declines locks in losses and risks missing the rebound. 
• The bigger risk is interrupting compounding by trying to avoid normal volatility.

Being underwater is uncomfortable but expected. The investors who do best treat drawdowns as the entry fee, not a reason to exit. Stay invested and let the long-term maths work.

This view is a bit too binary. 

There are many problems that don’t require one to be a user of the system — like consensus or improving snarks. That’s OK since they are core comp sci problems. 

However, the main issue today, is that many problems facing Ethereum are user experience issues caused by the platform itself. 

If the core developers are not using the platform — from an actual usage or building on top of perspective — then they cant properly prioritise the issues that need to be fixed. 

This is why there was so misplaced hype around long term strawman proposals vs fixing low hanging fruit (like sponsored transactions or increasing gas limits) that would immediately help users.

Core Developers, EF, everyone involved needs to treat Ethereum the network as a product and not an ideological-driven machine.
